topic: What a UK business should know before signing a new electricity contract

findings.claim: Ofgem defines the main UK business energy contract types: fixed-rate, variable-rate, deemed-rate, out-of-contract, rollover/evergreen and flexible (structured). They differ in price certainty and risk.
findings.evidence: Ofgem: fixed-rate contracts "fix the price of unit rates and standing charges for the length of the contract", so the cost per kWh stays the same whatever happens to wholesale prices. With variable-rate contracts the price "can increase or decrease during the contract period", for example when wholesale prices change. Rollover/evergreen contracts renew automatically at the end of a fixed term if no new arrangement is made or no switch happens. The new term is usually 12 months and "may be on a higher rate". Ofgem also says suppliers may not offer all contract types.
findings.limitations: Ofgem's descriptions are brief. They give no figures on how much more deemed or out-of-contract rates cost. The page shows no date.

findings.claim: Deemed and out-of-contract rates are default states, not products you choose. They arise when no contract has been agreed, and they are usually more expensive than negotiated fixed-term contracts.
findings.evidence: Ofgem: you are put on a deemed contract automatically when you move into new premises without arranging a formal contract, and also if your supplier goes out of business. Deemed rates are "usually higher than negotiated contract rates". Some suppliers move you to out-of-contract rates if your fixed-term contract ends without a new deal, and these are also usually more expensive than fixed-term contracts. Ofgem advises checking what happens at contract end (auto-renewal, out-of-contract or deemed rates). GLCG (a broker/consultancy blog) says the same: deemed contracts apply when you move in without arranging a contract, and out-of-contract applies when a fixed term ends with no new deal. It adds that the supplier will often move you to a very expensive variable rate, and suggests starting to look for a new deal 3–6 months before expiry.
findings.limitations: GLCG is a commercial broker blog (published 2026-09-01) and is not a regulator source. Its 3–6 month advice is its own recommendation.

findings.claim: Fixed-term contracts give budget certainty but little flexibility. Variable contracts give flexibility but expose the buyer to market volatility. Flexible/pass-through contracts give the most control and the most risk. A "fixed" contract may not fix every part of the bill.
findings.evidence: GLCG on fixed contracts: they are typically 1–3 years, protect against wholesale spikes and make budgeting simple. The buyer does not benefit if prices fall, is locked in, and exit fees can be substantial. Many "fixed" contracts let suppliers pass on unexpected increases in non-commodity costs, so check for change-event or pass-through clauses. GLCG on variable contracts: the unit price follows wholesale market moves and is often adjusted monthly. The buyer can benefit from falls but faces surges that make budgeting hard. GLCG on flexible purchasing (pass-through) contracts: energy is bought in smaller blocks over the contract period, so the buyer can target market lows and costs are more transparent. These contracts need active management, carry higher risk and are not suitable for most SMEs. In a fully fixed contract the supplier bundles estimated non-commodity costs (network, levies) into the rate. In a pass-through contract they are charged at actual cost, which gives transparency but less budget certainty. Ofgem says flexible (structured) contracts suit large, high-usage businesses. Instead of locking in a price, they let companies buy energy in smaller portions when market conditions are better.
findings.limitations: The pros and cons come mainly from GLCG, a commercial source. Ofgem gives only a short description of flexible contracts. Neither source gives a precise regulatory definition of "pass-through" as distinct from "flexible".

findings.claim: Contracts can be arranged directly or through third-party intermediaries (brokers, consultants, price comparison sites). This brings cost-transparency and redress considerations, and there is no cooling-off period.
findings.evidence: Ofgem: you can arrange a contract yourself or use a broker, consultant or price comparison service (third-party intermediaries). Brokers charge, either an upfront fee or, more commonly, a commission paid by the supplier you choose. If a supplier pays the broker, the broker must belong to an approved redress scheme. Ofgem points to the Energy Ombudsman broker register and the UIA accredited list. Comparison sites may cover only part of the market and may earn commission. Ofgem also says: "there is no cooling-off period after you agree to your contract". It says to check whether broker fees or commissions are included in the price. GLCG says brokers can analyse consumption, explain contract structures, spot hidden charges and negotiate with several suppliers.
findings.limitations: Ofgem does not describe a separate "broker-brokered" contract type. Brokerage is a way of buying, and the underlying contract is still one of the types above.

findings.claim: Protections vary by business size. Microbusinesses get extra protections, mostly for evergreen contracts, so the risks of rollover and default rates differ by customer size.
findings.evidence: Ofgem: a microbusiness has fewer than 10 employees and turnover or balance sheet of no more than £2 million, or uses up to 100,000 kWh/year of electricity. Suppliers must give clear contract information and renewal price information before the contract ends. For evergreen contracts only, termination notice is limited to 30 days and requests to end must be acknowledged within 5 working days. Small and large businesses get different protections.
findings.limitations: Thresholds are as stated on the Ofgem page, which shows no date. Check current rules before relying on them.

findings.claim: Microbusinesses get specific protections at renewal and on ending a contract, but the notice-period and acknowledgement protections in Ofgem's guidance apply to evergreen contracts only.
findings.evidence: Ofgem: microbusiness suppliers must give clear contract information and renewal price information before the contract ends. For evergreen contracts only, termination notice is limited to 30 days and requests to end must be acknowledged within 5 working days. Citizens Advice: for a microbusiness on an evergreen (no end date) contract, you "might have to give up to 30 days' notice" before switching. Ofgem also says that a contract's end-of-term outcome (auto-renewal, out-of-contract or deemed rates) should be checked before agreeing.
findings.limitations: These are summaries of guidance, not licence condition text. Neither page cites SLC numbers. Small and large businesses get different, weaker protections. Ofgem's page shows no date.

findings.claim: Supplier renewal prompts, rollover periods and exit fees: for microbusinesses on fixed terms, suppliers should contact the customer about 3 months before the end. Once the fixed term has ended the customer can switch at any time without a fee or notice. Leaving early can mean an exit fee.
findings.evidence: Citizens Advice: "If your fixed term is ending soon, your supplier should let you know your switching options. They should contact you about 3 months before the end of your contract. If they don't, you can complain." If the fixed term has ended you can switch at any time with no fee and no notice. A contract may give a 'roll-over period' of no more than 12 months. Without one, or once it has ended, you are on an 'out-of-contract' tariff. You can switch from a roll-over period or out-of-contract tariff without a fee or notice. Switching before the end of a fixed term "might" mean an exit fee, so check when you can switch fee-free and whether the saving outweighs the fee. A deemed tariff also usually carries no switching fee or notice. Ofgem says rollover/evergreen contracts renew for a fixed term, usually 12 months, possibly at a higher rate.
findings.limitations: Citizens Advice's advice is framed for microbusinesses and for England. It gives no exit-fee amounts or calculation method, which are set by each contract. The page shows no date.

findings.claim: Switching process and contract formation: a business switch normally completes within 5 working days. There is no cooling-off period, and a verbal agreement can be binding.
findings.evidence: Citizens Advice: "You'll be switched to your new supplier within 5 working days", or on a specific date if requested. There is no cooling-off period when you switch, and "if you change your mind you might have to pay a termination fee". Business contracts are binding if agreed over the phone, so no signature is needed. Most business suppliers offer no cooling-off period. Ask for the contract in writing. Take meter readings on switch day and send them to both companies. Ofgem likewise says there is no cooling-off period after you agree a contract.
findings.limitations: The 5-working-day timeline is from Citizens Advice's consumer guidance. The task also asked about objection rights, and no source read covers supplier objections to a switch. The page shows no date.

findings.claim: Broker transparency rules: microbusinesses must be told broker pay before agreeing. Ofgem has extended broker-fee disclosure to all non-domestic customers, and requires redress-scheme membership for brokers on Small Business contracts.
findings.evidence: Citizens Advice: for microbusinesses working with a supplier-paid broker, the broker must disclose how much the supplier pays them before the contract is agreed. Terms and conditions, including any broker fee, should arrive within 10 days of agreeing. Brokers paid by the supplier must be registered with the Energy Ombudsman or UIA. Ofgem press release (5 April 2024): the requirement for a contract's principal terms to clearly display broker fees was to be expanded from Micro Business consumers to all non-domestic customers. It applies to contracts signed on and from 1 October 2024, and suppliers must make the information available on request. From December 2024 suppliers may only work with TPIs that are redress-scheme members when securing Small Business contracts.
findings.limitations: The Ofgem press release says some measures were "expected" by the end of 2024. It does not confirm they came into force, so check current licence conditions. The 10-day figure comes from Citizens Advice.

findings.claim: Ofgem Standards of Conduct now apply to all non-domestic customers, and dispute-resolution access was widened. Microbusiness and Small Business definitions are set out by Ofgem and in the press release notes.
findings.evidence: Ofgem press release (5 April 2024): from 1 July 2024 the Standards of Conduct were expanded to apply to all businesses of any size, not just Micro Business consumers. A new licence rule requires suppliers to signpost Micro Business consumers to Citizens Advice and Citizens Advice Scotland. This applies to Small Business consumers from December 2024, subject to the new definition entering legislation. Microbusiness: electricity use under 100,000 kWh a year, gas use under 293,000 kWh a year, or fewer than 10 employees with annual turnover not exceeding 2 million Euros (£1.716m on 22 March 2024). Small business (Energy Ombudsman coverage): fewer than 50 employees and £6.5 million turnover or £5 million balance sheet total, or 200,000 kWh electricity or 500,000 kWh gas a year. Ofgem's guidance page states the microbusiness test as fewer than 10 employees and turnover or balance sheet of no more than £2 million, or use of up to 100,000 kWh a year of electricity or 293,000 kWh a year of gas. Citizens Advice says microbusinesses get extra protections when switching.
findings.limitations: The press release is dated April 2024. The two Ofgem pages state the microbusiness definition slightly differently (Euro versus pound turnover, "less than" versus "up to" thresholds). Check the licence condition for the exact definition. No licence condition numbers are cited.

findings.claim: A business electricity bill splits into commodity costs (the energy itself, which tracks the wholesale market) and non-commodity costs (network, levies, supplier operating costs). Fixed contracts bundle the non-commodity costs into the rate, while pass-through contracts charge them at actual cost.
findings.evidence: GLCG: commodity costs are the price of the energy and "fluctuate with the wholesale market". Non-commodity costs include network maintenance fees, government levies for green initiatives and supplier operating costs, and can make up over half of the total bill. Bill line items include transmission and distribution charges (TNUoS and DUoS), balancing services (BSUoS), the Climate Change Levy (CCL), and Renewables Obligation (RO) and Feed-in Tariff (FiT) levies. "In a fully fixed contract, the supplier estimates these costs and bundles them into your rate. In a pass-through contract, these are charged at their actual cost, which provides transparency but reduces budget certainty." GLCG also warns that "fixed" does not always mean the whole bill is fixed. Many fixed contracts let suppliers pass on unexpected increases in non-commodity costs, so check for change-event or pass-through clauses. Ofgem says fixed-rate contracts fix unit rates and standing charges for the contract length, so the cost per kWh stays the same whatever wholesale prices do. It also says flexible (structured) contracts, for large users, buy energy in portions when market conditions are better.
findings.limitations: The component breakdown and the fixed versus pass-through treatment come from GLCG, a commercial consultancy blog. No Ofgem, NESO or network-operator page on business bill components was opened, so this is not an official breakdown. The percentage split of a bill and the exact negotiability of each element depend on the contract.

findings.claim: The Climate Change Levy applies to business (non-domestic) electricity and gas. HMRC publishes its rates by year, with reduced rates for Climate Change Agreement holders.
findings.evidence: GOV.UK (HMRC, last updated 27 Nov 2025): suppliers are responsible for charging the correct levy. The electricity main rate is £0.00775 per kWh from 1 April 2023 to 2025, £0.00801 from 1 April 2026 and £0.00827 from 1 April 2027. The gas rate is £0.00672 from April 2023, £0.00775 for 2024 and 2025, £0.00801 from April 2026 and £0.00827 from April 2027. Climate change agreement holders get a 92% discount on electricity, and 88% or 89% on gas depending on the year. Rates do not apply to domestic consumers or to charities for non-business use. The VAT notice adds that the levy is chargeable on industrial and commercial supply (agriculture, industry, commerce, public administration, other services). It excludes small amounts of energy (de minimis). The value of a supply for VAT purposes includes CCL where appropriate.
findings.limitations: The rate table was last updated 27 Nov 2025, so check GOV.UK for later changes. The 2026 and 2027 rates are as published on that page. The page does not say how contracts treat CCL, though tax changes are normally passed through.

findings.claim: VAT on business energy: the standing charge is treated as part of the supply for VAT purposes, so it takes the same VAT rate as the electricity. Qualifying use gets the reduced rate and non-qualifying use gets the standard rate. Pure network or meter charges made without a supply of electricity are standard-rated.
findings.evidence: HMRC VAT Notice 701/19: gas and electricity bills include a variable consumption charge and a fixed standing charge. "For VAT purposes it is regarded as part of the charge for a supply of gas or electricity, even though it is shown separately on bills." Where the supply is for qualifying use, the whole bill including the standing charge is taxed at the reduced rate. The supply of electricity for qualifying use is taxed at the reduced rate. Where a price covers electricity and standing or other charges, the whole supply takes the reduced rate. Charges for use of transmission or distribution lines, transformers or meters, without any supply of electricity, are always standard-rated. Wholesale electricity contracts are standard-rated. The page shows a temporary zero rate of VAT for domestic supplies and other qualifying use. It was announced on 21 July 2026 and extended at Budget 2026 from 31 March to 30 June 2027.
findings.limitations: The extract was shortened and the specific percentage rates were not visible in the text I read. I make no claim about the standard rate. The section defining "qualifying use" (section 3, de minimis and charity/domestic criteria) was omitted from the extract. The zero-rate announcement is described on the page as covering domestic supplies and other qualifying use, and it is unclear whether it covers ordinary business supplies. The page shows a last-updated date of 28 Oct 2026.

findings.claim: Ofgem does not license or regulate energy brokers (third-party intermediaries, TPIs). It sets voluntary principles and requires broker costs passed through the bill to be disclosed in the supplier's Principal Terms. Brokers paid directly by the business need not appear in those terms.
findings.evidence: Ofgem's TPI guidance (14 Oct 2022): "Ofgem do not regulate energy brokers" and "does not license TPIs but has set out voluntary principles": Honesty, Respect, Accuracy (say how much of the market was searched), Transparency (make the customer aware of all principal terms, including services and how they pay for them, directly or indirectly), Customer-focused (record and investigate complaints) and Professionalism. TPIs include switching sites, brokers and procurement firms. A TPI may be paid directly by the customer (flat fee, charge per trade) or indirectly, through a supplier payment added to the bill. TPI costs included in the supplier bill "must be provided to all businesses via the Principal Terms and upon request". Directly paid broker fees need not be declared in the supplier's principal terms. Supplier in-house sales teams need not disclose commission. Because commission is based on consumption, a customer who uses more than estimated pays on actual consumption. Ofgem advises asking a TPI which suppliers it will approach, how many offers it will give, what services it provides during the contract and how it is paid. TPIs must also comply with the Business Protection from Misleading Marketing Regulations, and Ofgem can seek court injunctions for breaches. Ofgem's 5 April 2024 press release adds that broker fees must be displayed in contracts' principal terms for all non-domestic customers, for contracts signed on and from 1 October 2024.
findings.limitations: The TPI guidance dates from October 2022, so some details may have changed (for example the 2024 expansion of disclosure to all non-domestic customers). Ofgem says it cannot require brokers to repay past undisclosed commission, and warns of scammers claiming otherwise. It notes recovery may be possible only through litigation (get independent legal advice).

findings.claim: Supplier-paid brokers must belong to a redress scheme (the Energy Ombudsman, the UIA or, per Citizens Advice, the DRO). A business should check registration before signing and be told in writing how the broker is paid.
findings.evidence: Citizens Advice: "If your broker is paid by your supplier they must be registered" with the Energy Ombudsman or the Utilities Intermediaries Association (UIA). Its problems page also lists the Dispute Resolution Ombudsman (DRO). "If your broker isn't registered you won't be able to complain." Each scheme's website has a register or accredited-member list. Microbusiness customers must be told what the supplier pays the broker before agreeing a contract. Terms should arrive within 10 days of agreeing. Phone agreements are binding, so ask for information in writing. Ofgem says: "Because there is no cooling-off period after you agree to your contract, it's important you make sure you use a trustworthy broker", and points to the Energy Ombudsman broker register and the UIA list. Ofgem says brokers' fees may be an upfront fee or, more usually, supplier commission.
findings.limitations: Citizens Advice mentions the DRO in one page and only the Energy Ombudsman and UIA in another, so the list may vary. Ofgem says it cannot approve redress schemes. The Citizens Advice pages show no date. Neither source gives UIA code-of-practice detail, as the UIA site was not read.

findings.claim: Complaint and escalation route: complain to the supplier or broker first, then the Energy Ombudsman after 8 weeks or a deadlock letter. Small businesses became eligible for broker and supplier disputes from 19 December 2024.
findings.evidence: Energy Ombudsman (page updated 2026-04-02): from 19 December 2024 small businesses can get free dispute resolution for disputes with a broker/TPI, where the business has fewer than 50 employees and turnover of at most £6.5 million or a balance sheet total of £5.0 million, or electricity use of no more than 200,000 kWh a year, or gas use of no more than 500,000 kWh a year. You must use the broker's or supplier's complaints process first. The Ombudsman can then help after 8 weeks or once a deadlock letter has been issued. Process: raise it with the broker, register the dispute, review any early resolution offer, evidence within 14 days, a decision, then 28 days for the broker to implement. Remedies: practical action, an apology, a payment of up to £10,000, and recommendations. It cannot fine or punish. It cannot rule on commercial decisions or on non-gas/electricity services such as LPG. It only handles brokers that have joined its scheme. Citizens Advice: for supplier complaints, 8 weeks or a deadlock letter, and 1 year from a deadlock letter to complain. Ofgem's April 2024 release says Small Businesses can resolve disputes about brokers with schemes such as the Energy Ombudsman and UIA, and that suppliers must signpost microbusinesses to Citizens Advice.
findings.limitations: The Energy Ombudsman page applies the eligibility test as quoted. It does not say whether a business must meet more than one criterion, though the wording uses "AND" and "OR". Citizens Advice's guidance is for England and for small and microbusinesses. Larger businesses may not qualify. Complaint wait times are those stated on each page.

findings.claim: Checking the supplier: Ofgem says a supplier is not obliged to supply a business and may choose customers by factors such as size or credit rating. Checks include contract end-of-term treatment and what happens if the supplier fails.
findings.evidence: Ofgem TPI guidance: "There is no obligation for a supplier to supply you – a supplier may determine which customers they choose to supply by factors such as size of supply or your credit rating." There are very few published business prices, so you need to ask suppliers for quotes. A contract can last multiple years and may have an early termination fee. Ofgem's business-contract page says you are placed on deemed rates if your supplier goes out of business, and to check what happens at the end of the contract. Citizens Advice advises that if your supplier goes bust, you should not switch tariff or supplier until your account has moved to the new supplier, because switching earlier can make it harder to get money you are owed. It also advises comparing as many suppliers as possible and asking for the full terms and conditions.
findings.limitations: No source read here covers supplier financial-resilience checks (for example Ofgem's financial responsibility or capital adequacy rules, credit ratings, or customer-service league tables). This finding is only about what the sources say on supplier choice and supplier failure.

findings.claim: Half-hourly settlement reform affects business electricity customers. Suppliers are migrating meters to market-wide half-hourly settlement (MHHS), so settlement will use actual half-hourly consumption rather than estimates or monthly readings.
findings.evidence: Elexon (page updated 2026-09-07): MHHS means settlement is based on "actual consumption for each half-hour of the electricity day, in place of estimates or monthly readings". Suppliers began migrating customers' meters from 22 October 2025. Elexon expects to have accepted about 80 per cent of meters by October 2026 and to complete implementation in May 2027. Key milestones: an 18-month migration for Unmetered Supplies and Advanced Metering Systems, which "are normally used by larger non-domestic consumers", starting 22 October 2025; an 18-month migration for smart and non-smart meters, also starting 22 October 2025; full transition complete 7 May 2027; and a cut-over to a shorter settlement timetable on 2 July 2027. Settlement currently takes 14 months and is planned to drop to four months. Elexon says granular data lets suppliers develop products that reward flexible use.
findings.limitations: This is an industry-facing Elexon page, not customer-facing guidance. It does not say how MHHS changes business contract prices or what customers must do, and it gives no customer-specific meter or contract-capacity guidance. The page does not cover contract capacity, usage-data preparation or purchase timing.

findings.claim: Green or renewable tariff claims can be checked against the REGO scheme. A REGO certificate shows that one MWh of electricity was generated from renewable sources, and suppliers must disclose their fuel mix annually.
findings.evidence: Ofgem: the REGO scheme "provides transparency to consumers about the proportion of electricity that suppliers source from renewable electricity". One REGO is issued per megawatt hour (MWh) of eligible renewable output. The primary use is Fuel Mix Disclosure (FMD), which requires licensed GB electricity suppliers to disclose to potential and existing customers the mix of fuels (coal, gas, nuclear, renewable, other) used to generate the electricity they supply. Ofgem administers the scheme for GB on behalf of the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero. EU Guarantees of Origin are no longer recognised for GB FMD, FIT annual levelisation or CfD from the disclosure period beginning 1 April 2023.
findings.limitations: The Ofgem page explains the REGO scheme and FMD but does not give business-specific advice on verifying a supplier's green tariff, such as whether a tariff is REGO-backed. No ASA or CMA green claims guidance was read. The page shows no date.

findings.claim: ESOS (the Energy Savings Opportunity Scheme) is a compliance obligation for qualifying large undertakings that involves energy audits and a notification to the Environment Agency. It is separate from the choice of energy contract, though ESOS audits use measured consumption data.
findings.evidence: GOV.UK ESOS phase 3 guidance (Environment Agency as UK scheme administrator, last updated 2026-07-30): qualification is based on status on the qualification date. A qualifying organisation must carry out energy audits, or use alternative compliance routes (ISO 50001, DEC, GDA), complete an ESOS report, have a director review the findings, and submit a notification of compliance through the online system. Audits must be based, so far as reasonably practicable, on verifiable consumption data measured in energy units (not spend) over 12 consecutive months, and energy audits must be reviewed by an ESOS lead assessor unless total energy consumption is under 40,000 kWh. EPCs are not a valid compliance route. The page says the remaining phase 3 deadline is to submit the second progress update report by 5 December 2026, and refers readers to separate Phase 4 guidance for the current qualification and compliance requirements. Participating in other schemes does not automatically count as ESOS compliance.
findings.limitations: I read only the phase 3 guidance, which says phase 4 requirements (including the 2026 amendment to the regulations) are in separate guidance that I did not open. I therefore make no claim about the phase 4 qualification date, deadlines or thresholds. The page does not define a "large undertaking" in the extract shown.

findings.claim: Timing and data preparation before signing: know the contract end date and notice position, start renewal work early, and have accurate consumption information ready. This avoids defaulting to expensive out-of-contract or deemed rates and affects quotes and broker commission.
findings.evidence: GLCG advises identifying the contract end date and notice period and starting to look for a new deal at least three to six months in advance, using smart meter data to understand usage patterns. Citizens Advice says the supplier should contact microbusinesses about 3 months before the end of a fixed term, and that customers need to check contract terms, end date, standing charges, unit costs and annual usage when preparing to switch. Ofgem's TPI guidance says commission is based on consumption, so if actual use exceeds the estimate the customer pays on actual consumption, and estimates should be as accurate as possible. Ofgem also says suppliers can decide whether to supply based on size of supply or credit rating.
findings.limitations: The 3–6 month figure is a commercial broker recommendation (GLCG), not regulator guidance. No source read covers contract capacity (for example availability charges), or half-hourly meter-specific preparation.

findings.claim: TNUoS (transmission network charges) is set by NESO under its licence and the CUSC. Total revenue recovered is rising, and a large 'demand residual' element is passed through to demand customers. NESO forecasts further increases for 2027/28.
findings.evidence: NESO webinar slides (May 2026), 'Initial TNUoS Tariffs for 2027/28': NESO is forecasting and setting TNUoS "to recover around £9bn of revenue per year from generators and demand; in addition to BSUoS". NESO has a licence and CUSC obligation to publish quarterly TNUoS forecasts and an annual Five-Year View. Final 2027/28 tariffs are due by 31 January 2027 and take effect from 1 April 2027. Total TNUoS revenue is forecast at £9.11bn for 2027/28, up £1.50bn on the 2026/27 final tariffs, driven mainly by onshore transmission owner allowed revenues (up £1.58bn). Demand revenue is forecast at £7.73bn, up £1.35bn. The demand residual tariff is forecast to be 21% higher than 2026/27, and demand residual charges are expressed as £/day by charging band. The average half-hourly (HH) demand tariff is forecast at £3.48/kW (up £0.69/kW) and the average non-half-hourly (NHH) tariff at 0.48p/kWh (up 0.10p/kWh). TNUoS on the average consumer electricity bill is forecast at £96.85, up £13.61. The slides also say substantial change to the charging methodology (the Reform of National Pricing programme) is expected but is not included in the forecast.
findings.limitations: These are initial forecasts (May 2026), not final tariffs, and are written for industry participants. The slides give no explanation of how suppliers pass these charges into a business contract. The £96.85 figure refers to the average consumer bill, not a business bill. No Ofgem page was read for DUoS. The page shows no formal date beyond 'May 2026'.

findings.claim: BSUoS (balancing services charges) is set and published by NESO as a fixed tariff in advance, and since 1 April 2023 it has been recovered only from final demand, including suppliers.
findings.evidence: NESO BSUoS page: "The BSUoS charge recovers the cost of day-to-day operation including the cost of balancing the electricity transmission system." It applies to final demand sites, suppliers and directly-connected transmission demand, and not to generators, DNOs, embedded generators or interconnectors, with exemptions. CMP308 and CMP361 came into effect on 1 April 2023: CMP308 defined that BSUoS charges are recovered solely from final demand, and CMP361 introduced an ex-ante fixed BSUoS tariff. Fixed tariffs 7 and 8 for 2026/27 were published on 29 December 2025.
findings.limitations: The page does not give the tariff level and does not say how a supplier passes BSUoS on to business contracts. The extract shows no single publication date for the page.

findings.claim: Renewables Obligation (RO): an obligation on suppliers, not a charge set directly on business customers. It is closed to new capacity but still operates.
findings.evidence: Ofgem: the RO closed to all new generating capacity on 1 April 2017. It places an annual obligation on electricity suppliers to present ROCs per MWh supplied in each obligation period (1 April – 31 March), or to pay into a buy-out fund, or to do a combination. Ofgem accredits stations, issues and revokes ROCs, receives buy-out payments and redistributes the funds. The page says nothing about how suppliers recover this cost from customers.
findings.limitations: The Ofgem page describes the scheme mechanics only. It does not say that the cost is passed to non-domestic customers, nor give the obligation level or the cost per MWh. The same applies to the Feed-in Tariff, CfD levy and capacity market: no official page covering them was read, so this finding should not be treated as corroboration of the GLCG list for those items. The page shows no date.

findings.claim: Comparison with the GLCG breakdown from earlier research: the official sources read partly corroborate it, since NESO describes TNUoS and BSUoS as network and system charges set centrally. They do not corroborate its claim that these costs are charged at actual cost under pass-through contracts, or its list of levies.
findings.evidence: GLCG lists TNUoS/DUoS, BSUoS, CCL and RO/FiT as bill line items, bundled into the rate in fully fixed contracts and passed through at actual cost in pass-through contracts. The NESO pages confirm that TNUoS and BSUoS are set by NESO, that BSUoS is recovered from final demand and suppliers via a fixed tariff, and that TNUoS revenue is rising. Ofgem confirms the RO places the obligation on suppliers. GOV.UK (read in an earlier task) sets CCL rates. None of these official pages says how a supplier passes the charges through in a particular contract type.
findings.limitations: This is a synthesis across sources. None of the official pages addresses fixed versus pass-through contract treatment, so that part of GLCG's account remains from a commercial source only.

findings.claim: Ofgem's business switching guidance: when you can switch depends on the contract type. Fixed-rate contracts usually cannot be left early without an exit fee or an agreed termination clause, though a pre-expiry 'switching window' may allow a fee-free switch. Variable, evergreen, out-of-contract and deemed customers can switch at any time. The existing supplier may object to a switch, for example if you owe it money.
findings.evidence: Ofgem: for fixed-rate contracts, "Most suppliers will not let you switch before the end of your contract unless you have already agreed a termination clause or pay an exit fee." Fixed-rate contracts include a 'switching window', a set period to renew or say you intend to leave, which opens a few months before the end. You can sometimes switch in that window without a fee. With a variable-rate contract, including a rolling or 'evergreen' contract, out-of-contract rates or a deemed-rate contract, "you can switch to a new supplier at any time". You must give the new supplier your annual consumption and meter details before signing. "Your existing supplier may object to your switch, for example if you owe them money. If this happens, get in touch with them as soon as possible." Customers moving premises are responsible for energy used before a new contract starts and may be put on a deemed-rate contract. Citizens Advice (earlier source) also notes a switch to the new supplier completes within 5 working days.
findings.limitations: The Ofgem page lists only a debt objection as an example and does not set out the full list of permitted objection grounds, nor give the non-domestic switching timeline. The 5-working-day figure comes from Citizens Advice. The Ofgem page shows no date, and no licence condition numbers are given on it.

findings.claim: Termination-notice rules for microbusinesses have changed in two steps. Since 30 April 2015 the maximum notice was 30 days. Since 1 October 2022 suppliers cannot require microbusinesses to give notice to switch, except on evergreen contracts.
findings.evidence: Ofgem factsheet (29 July 2015): since 30 April 2015 the maximum notice period for terminating a micro-business contract was reduced from 90 to 30 days. Suppliers must include current prices, new prices and annual consumption on renewal letters for fixed-term contracts. They must take all reasonable steps to acknowledge termination notice within five working days of receipt. CMS law-firm summary of Ofgem's Microbusiness Strategic Review decision (28 March 2022): the decision prohibited suppliers from requiring microbusinesses to give prior notice of termination, except for Evergreen Contracts, in force from 1 October 2022. The rationale was to ease switching. Retaining the evergreen exemption typically lets suppliers offer non-fixed-term options at lower cost than deemed or out-of-contract rates. Ofgem's current business-contract guidance (read earlier) still states the 30-day limit and 5-working-day acknowledgement as applying to evergreen contracts only.
findings.limitations: The CMS page is a law-firm summary of the Ofgem decision, not the decision itself. The 2015 factsheet is dated and pre-dates the 2022 change, so the 2022 decision supersedes it for fixed-term contracts.

findings.claim: Licence references and related 2022 changes: the Principal Terms obligation is in supply licence condition (SLC) 7A. The 2022 decision tightened principal-terms disclosure (including brokerage costs) and required suppliers to use only brokers in a qualifying ADR scheme.
findings.evidence: CMS summary: the existing obligation to bring Principal Terms to the microbusiness's attention pre-contract is under SLC 7A.4, and the decision added a post-contract written requirement. Purely signposting Principal Terms during a sales call is not sufficient, and verbally agreed contracts require clear explanation of the Principal Terms. Brokerage costs must be shown via the Principal Terms as a total cost in pounds and pence over the contract duration, effective from 1 October 2022. A new supply licence condition requires suppliers to work only with brokers in a qualifying ADR scheme, effective from 1 December 2022. A proposed 1–14 day cooling-off period was not implemented. Ofgem's April 2024 press release (read earlier) later extended broker-fee display in principal terms to all non-domestic customers.
findings.limitations: These references come from a law-firm summary. The licence text itself was not read. The SLC reference for the termination-notice change is not stated on that page. The 2024 extension is described in the Ofgem press release as expected for contracts signed on and from 1 October 2024.

findings.claim: ESOS phase 4: qualification is assessed on 31 December 2026, and the compliance notification deadline is 5 December 2027. Phase 4 has stricter compliance routes and more action-plan reporting.
findings.evidence: GOV.UK ESOS guidance (DESNZ/Environment Agency, last updated 2 September 2026): ESOS is a mandatory energy assessment scheme for qualifying UK organisations, with an assessment every 4 years covering buildings, industrial processes and transport. "Your organisation qualifies for ESOS phase 4 if, on 31 December 2026, it meets the ESOS definition of a large undertaking." Corporate groups qualify if at least one UK group member is a large undertaking. The deadline for the phase 4 notification of compliance, submitted through MESOS, is 5 December 2027. For phase 3 the qualification date was 31 December 2022. Phase 4 changes: DECs and Green Deal assessments can no longer be used as alternative compliance routes. Progress against action plan commitments must be included, and unmet commitments explained. Compliance must use an energy audit or ISO 50001 certification (issued after 5 December 2023 and valid at 5 December 2027). A lead assessor must sign off unless total energy consumption is covered by ISO 50001 or is less than 40,000 kWh. Audit data must cover a 12-month period beginning no earlier than 6 December 2022, and audits must include site visits. A board-level director must sign off. Regulators may impose civil sanctions including financial penalties. Phase 3 participants must submit an annual progress update by 5 December 2026. The regulations were amended by the Energy Savings Opportunities Scheme (Amendment) Regulations 2026.
findings.limitations: The extract I read did not include the definition and thresholds of a 'large undertaking' (employee, turnover or balance sheet figures), which the page says are in section 1 of the phase 4 compliance guidance. I did not open that guidance. Check it before relying on the thresholds. ESOS is about energy assessment, not about contract choice.

findings.claim: The only current government energy-cost support found is the British Industrial Competitiveness Scheme (BICS), a targeted scheme for eligible manufacturers. It is not a general support scheme for all business electricity buyers.
findings.evidence: GOV.UK press release (1 October 2026): applications opened for BICS, with eligible manufacturers urged to apply by 30 November to receive support from April 2027. Eligible businesses in England, Scotland and Wales will be exempt from paying the indirect costs of the Renewables Obligation, Feed-in Tariffs and Capacity Market. The release says BICS will cut manufacturers' electricity costs by up to 25 percent, and that the percentage discount depends on the underlying electricity price each company pays. It is aimed at more than 10,000 manufacturing businesses in the Modern Industrial Strategy's eight high-growth sectors and the foundational industries that supply them. Businesses confirmed as eligible and applying this year are also in line for an additional lump-sum payment equivalent to around a year's relief. The release also refers to extended support through the British Industry Supercharger for energy-intensive industries, and says the Northern Ireland Executive will receive funding for an equivalent scheme, subject to business case development. The earlier VAT Notice 701/19 (read in a previous task) describes the Energy Bill Relief Scheme as applying to energy use from 1 October 2022 up to and including 31 March 2023.
findings.limitations: The BICS source is a press release. Detailed eligibility criteria are in separate GOV.UK guidance for applicants that I did not read. No page I read names or describes a successor to the Energy Bill Discount Scheme, and I found no GOV.UK page stating whether a general successor exists. The VAT notice also mentions a temporary VAT zero rate for domestic supplies and other qualifying use, but I cannot confirm from it whether that covers ordinary business electricity.

English
Cymraeg
Newid yr iaith i'r Gymraeg
Get a business energy contract

Types of business energy contracts you can get, and how to set one up.

Contents
How business sizes affect energy contracts
Types of business contracts
Get help to arrange your contract

If you’re starting a new business, moving premises or changing energy suppliers, you’ll need to set up a business energy contract. The terms, pricing and regulations differ from standard home energy contracts.

Find out more about what to do when moving premises or switching business contracts.

The type of contract you can get usually depends on the size of your business, and how much energy you use. Before you agree to a contract, it’s important to know:

what type of contract it is
how long the term is
if there are any fees involved, for example those agreed in special clauses in your contract
what protections you have
if any broker fees or commissions are included in the price

It’s also important to know what happens at the end of your contract, for example if it will automatically renew, or if you will move to out-of-contract or deemed rates.

If you run your business from home

If you work from home you are probably on a domestic energy contract. Check with your energy supplier to make sure.

How business sizes affect energy contracts

The type of contract you need if you run a business will depend on the:

number of people you employ
income your business makes over a year
amount of electricity or gas your business uses a year

Different sizes of businesses get different protections.

Microbusinesses

To qualify as a microbusiness, you must have fewer than 10 employees and an annual turnover or balance sheet total of no more than £2 million.

You can also qualify if you use up to 100,000 kWh per year (electricity) or up to 293,000 kWh per year (gas).

If you are a microbusiness, you have extra protections when arranging or renewing an energy contract. Your energy supplier must:

provide clear information about your contract
limit termination notice periods to 30 days (evergreen contracts only)
acknowledge requests to end a contract within 5 working days (evergreen contracts only)
provide information about renewal prices before your contract ends

Microbusinesses and small businesses can get support with their energy contracts from Citizens Advice. They can also get help with unresolved supplier complaints from the Energy Ombudsman.

Small businesses

To qualify as a small business, you must have 11 to 50 employees and an annual turnover of up to £6.5 million or balance sheet total of no more than £5 million.

You can also qualify if you use up to 200,000 kWh per year (electricity) or up to 500,000 kWh per year (gas).

Large businesses

To qualify as a large business, you must have 50 or more employees and an annual turnover of more than £6.5 million or balance sheet total of more than £5 million.

You can also qualify if you use more than 200,000 kWh per year (electricity) or more than 500,000 kWh per year (gas).

Some suppliers may use either your business size or your annual energy consumption when deciding which contract or protections apply.

Types of business contracts

There are a number of different types of business energy contracts. Energy suppliers may not offer all of them.

Fixed-rate contracts

Fixed rate contracts fix the price of unit rates and standing charges for the length of the contract. This means the cost per kWh remains the same no matter what happens to wholesale market prices.

Variable-rate contracts

With a variable-rate contract, the price you pay for energy can increase or decrease during the contract period. This may be because your prices change when the wholesale market prices change.

Deemed-rate contracts

You will be put on a deemed contract automatically when you move into a new premises without arranging a formal contract. Deemed rates are usually higher than negotiated contract rates.

You will also be put on a deemed rate if your energy supplier goes out of business.

Out of contract rates

Some suppliers move you onto out-of-contract rates if your fixed-term contract ends without you agreeing to a new deal. Like deemed rate contracts, these rates are usually more expensive than fixed-term contracts.

Rollover or evergreen contracts

Some contracts automatically renew at the end of a fixed term contract if you have not made a new arrangement, or switched to a new supplier. The new arrangement will be for a fixed term (usually 12 months), and may be on a higher rate.

Flexible contracts

Flexible contracts (sometimes called structured contracts) are suitable for large businesses that use a lot of energy. Rather than locking into a fixed price, they allow companies to buy energy in smaller portions when market conditions are better.

Get help to arrange your contract

You can arrange your business contract yourself, or you can use an energy broker, consultant or a price comparison service (also known as third-party intermediaries).

Using a price comparison service

Price comparison websites help you compare business gas and electricity contracts from different suppliers. Check which suppliers are included in the comparison, and whether the website compares the whole market or only a selection of suppliers. You should also check whether the website receives commission from energy suppliers or other sources.

Using an energy broker

Energy brokers can help you find a suitable contract for your business, and then negotiate with your chosen supplier. This can save you time and resources.

Brokers charge you for their services. Some charge an upfront fee, but most are paid a commission by the energy supplier you choose. If your broker is paid by an energy supplier, they must be a member of an approved redress scheme.

Before using one, check which scheme they belong to:

Energy Ombudsman broker register
Utilities Intermediaries Association (UIA) accredited member list

Because there is no cooling-off period after you agree to your contract, it’s important you make sure you use a trustworthy broker.

INSIGHTS
Business Energy Contract Types: How to Choose the Right Contract
Compare fixed, variable and flexible business energy contracts — and learn how to avoid costly deemed and rollover rates.
SEPTEMBER 1, 2026

Home » Business Energy Contract Types: How to Choose the Right Contract

Unlike your straightforward domestic energy bill, a business energy contract is a complex agreement filled with critical choices that can significantly impact your bottom line. Choosing the wrong one can mean overpaying by thousands, while the right one offers budget certainty and supports growth. Yet many businesses fall into expensive default rates simply because the options feel overwhelming.

This guide breaks down the jargon and clarifies the choices. We’ll walk through the main contract types, expose common myths, and give you a clear framework for deciding which path is right for your business.

What is a business energy contract?

Business energy contracts are generally less regulated than domestic tariffs, meaning suppliers have greater flexibility when setting prices and contract terms. This creates opportunities to secure competitive rates, but it also makes it more important to understand exactly what you’re agreeing to before signing.

Compare, switch and save today

Compare business energy, water and telecoms quotes from leading UK suppliers in minutes. It’s free, there’s no obligation, and it takes about a minute.

Most suppliers offer multiple business energy contract types to accommodate different levels of energy consumption, budget certainty and risk tolerance. Selecting the right contract depends on your operational needs, financial objectives, and how actively you want to manage energy purchasing throughout the contract period.

The core components of any business energy contract

Before diving into contract types, it’s essential to understand what you’re actually paying for. Every bill is split into two main parts:

Commodity costs: this is the price of the energy (gas or electricity) itself. It’s the part of your bill that fluctuates with the wholesale market.
Non-commodity costs: these are all the other charges required to get the energy from the power station to your premises. They include network maintenance fees, government levies for green initiatives and supplier operating costs. These charges can make up over half of your total bill and are a common source of confusion.

Understanding this split is crucial because different contracts handle these costs in different ways.

A deep dive into business energy contract types

Most business energy contracts fall into one of three main categories: fixed, variable or flexible. There are also a couple of default states you should actively avoid.

Fixed-rate contracts

This is the most common type of contract, especially for small to medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). You agree to a set price per unit (kWh) of energy for a defined period, typically one to three years.

Pros: offers budget certainty and protects you from sudden wholesale market price spikes. It simplifies financial planning.
Cons: you won’t benefit if market prices fall. You are locked in for the duration, and exit fees can be substantial.
Best for: businesses that need predictable costs and value stability over potential market savings. Think cafes, retail shops and small offices.

A common myth busted: “fixed” doesn’t always mean 100% of your bill is fixed. Many fixed-rate contracts allow suppliers to pass on unexpected increases in non-commodity costs. It’s vital to check the contract terms for clauses about change events or pass-through charges.

Variable-rate contracts

With a variable-rate contract, the unit price of your energy changes based on fluctuations in the wholesale market. The supplier adjusts your rate periodically, often monthly.

Pros: you can benefit from falling market prices without being locked into a high rate. They often offer more flexibility with shorter or no fixed terms.
Cons: you are exposed to market volatility. A sudden price surge can dramatically increase your bills, making budgeting difficult.
Best for: businesses with a higher risk appetite or those who believe the market is likely to fall. It can also be a short-term solution while waiting for better fixed-rate deals.
Flexible purchasing (or pass-through) contracts

These are more advanced contracts designed for large, energy-intensive businesses. Instead of buying all your energy in one go, you purchase it in smaller blocks throughout the contract period. This allows you to take advantage of market lows and manage risk more actively.

Pros: offers the potential for significant savings by buying energy strategically when prices are low. Provides greater transparency as commodity and non-commodity costs are often separated.
Cons: requires active management and a deep understanding of the energy market. It carries higher risk and is not suitable for most SMEs.
Best for: large industrial and manufacturing businesses with high energy consumption and dedicated resources to manage their energy procurement.
The expensive defaults: deemed and out-of-contract rates

These aren’t contracts you choose; they are states your business can fall into, and they are always costly.

Deemed contracts: if you move into a new business premises without arranging a contract beforehand, you’ll be placed on a deemed contract with the existing supplier. Ofgem confirms these rates are typically much higher than negotiated ones.
Out-of-contract and rollover contracts: this happens when your fixed-term contract ends and you haven’t agreed to a new one or switched suppliers. Your current supplier will often move you onto a very expensive variable rate. Some contracts include an auto-renewal clause, locking you into another term at uncompetitive rates if you don’t provide notice to terminate.

The key to avoiding these is proactive management: know your contract end date and start looking for a new deal at least three to six months in advance.

How to choose the right contract for your business

Selecting the optimal contract isn’t about finding the absolute cheapest unit rate. It’s about finding the best value and the right fit for your business’s operational needs and goals.

Assess your energy usage: do you operate at consistent times, or does your consumption fluctuate wildly? Smart meter data can provide powerful insights here. A business with predictable usage (like a 9-to-5 office) is a great candidate for a fixed rate. A business with seasonal peaks might explore different options.
Define your risk appetite: how important is budget certainty? If an unexpected 30% jump in your energy bill would be a serious problem, the safety of a fixed-rate contract is likely your best choice. If you have the cash flow to handle volatility and want to chase market lows, a variable rate could be considered.
Consider your business goals: are sustainability and reducing your carbon footprint a priority? If so, you might look specifically for green tariffs that guarantee your energy comes from renewable sources, or even explore a Power Purchase Agreement (PPA) if your consumption is large enough.
How long should a business energy contract be?

Contract length is another important consideration when comparing business energy contract types. Although one-, two- and three-year agreements remain the most common, the ideal term depends on market conditions, business stability and future plans.

One-year contracts

Shorter agreements provide greater flexibility and allow businesses to renegotiate sooner if market prices fall. However, they also expose organisations to more frequent renewals and potential price volatility.

Two-year contracts

Two-year contracts often strike a balance between pricing certainty and flexibility. Many businesses choose this option because it provides longer-term budget stability without committing to an extended agreement.

Three-year contracts and longer

Longer contracts may offer attractive pricing during favourable market conditions while reducing the administrative burden of regular renewals. However, businesses should carefully consider future expansion, relocation or operational changes before committing to longer terms, as early termination charges may apply.

Regardless of contract length, businesses should begin reviewing renewal options several months before expiry. Allowing sufficient time to compare suppliers and negotiate pricing significantly reduces the likelihood of being transferred onto expensive out-of-contract rates.

Understanding your bill: where the costs really are

A common point of frustration for business owners is an energy bill that seems disconnected from the rate they signed up for. This is almost always due to the impact of non-commodity costs.

Your bill will show the unit rate (commodity) you agreed to, but it will also include separate line items for:

Transmission and distribution charges (TNUoS & DUoS): the cost of using the national and local energy networks.
Balancing services (BSUoS): costs for keeping the national grid stable.
Climate Change Levy (CCL): a government tax on energy usage.
Renewables Obligation (RO) and Feed-in Tariff (FiT): levies that support large-scale and small-scale renewable energy generation.

In a fully fixed contract, the supplier estimates these costs and bundles them into your rate. In a pass-through contract, these are charged at their actual cost, which provides transparency but reduces budget certainty.

Watch out for red flags before you sign

The complexity of energy contracts can unfortunately be used to hide unfavourable terms. Before signing any new agreement, look carefully for these common pitfalls. A trusted independent consultant can be invaluable in spotting these clauses.

Should you use an energy broker?

Many businesses choose to work with an independent business energy broker or consultant when comparing business energy contract types. While this is not essential for every organisation, professional advice can simplify the procurement process and provide access to a broader range of supplier options.

An experienced broker can help analyse historical energy consumption, explain contract structures, identify hidden charges and negotiate pricing with multiple suppliers. This can be particularly valuable for businesses without dedicated procurement teams or those managing several commercial properties.

[...]
Understanding your business energy contract is the first step toward taking control of one of your most significant operational costs. By moving beyond just the headline unit price and considering your usage patterns, risk tolerance and the details in the fine print, you can make a strategic decision that benefits your business for years to come.

The next practical step is to identify your current contract’s end date and notice period. Put it in your calendar. This simple action is the key to avoiding expensive rollover rates and gives you the time you need to explore the market and find the contract that truly fits your business.

Which contract suits you?

Tell us how your business uses energy and we’ll put fixed, flexible and pass-through options side by side, with the real cost of each. No obligation.

Switching your business to a new energy supplier

This advice applies to England. See advice for
See advice for
Northern Ireland,
See advice for
Scotland,
See advice for
Wales

Help us improve our website

Take 5 minutes to tell us if you found what you needed on our website. Your feedback will help us give millions of people the information they need.

If you work from home

If your business is based from home, you'll usually be a domestic energy customer instead of a business customer. Check how to switch if you’re a domestic customer.

Switching your energy supplier could save you money but it can take time to organise.

You'll need to check some details about your current contract, including:

the terms of your current contract - including the end date

your standing charges and energy costs per unit - these are shown in kilowatt hours on your bill

your annual energy usage

If you’re a microbusiness you might get extra protections when switching. Check if your business is a microbusiness.

If you're not sure if your supplier should be treating you as a microbusiness, contact the Citizens Advice consumer service.

Important
If your energy supplier goes bust

Don’t switch tariff or supplier until your account is moved to the new supplier. You might find it harder to get any money you’re owed if you switch before this happens.

Read our advice about what to do if your energy supplier goes bust.

Check if you can switch

You'll normally be able to switch to a new business energy supplier if:

you're not tied in to your contract - it's important to check when your contract ends

you're on a tariff you didn't choose to be on, for example if you've taken over a new premises - you'll be on a 'deemed' tariff

the fixed term of your contract has ended

If you’re on a deemed tariff it’s worth switching - these are usually the most expensive tariffs. You usually won't need to pay a fee or give notice to switch.

If you think you should be able to switch but your supplier won't let you, contact the Citizens Advice consumer service.

If you're a microbusiness on a fixed-term contract

It’s usually best to wait until the end of your fixed-term contract before you switch.

If you want to switch before the end of your contract, you might have to pay a fee to leave your contract early - this is an ‘exit fee’.

If you’d have to pay an exit fee to switch, check:

when you’ll be able to switch without paying an exit fee

how much you’d save by switching - you might save more money, even if you have to pay an exit fee

If your contract has no end date, sometimes called an ‘evergreen contract’, you might have to give up to 30 days’ notice before you switch.

If your fixed term is ending soon, your supplier should let you know your switching options. They should contact you about 3 months before the end of your contract. If they don’t, you can complain to your supplier.

If your fixed term has already ended you can switch at any time. You won’t need to pay your supplier a fee to switch and you won’t need to give notice.

Your contract might give you a 'roll-over period' to agree a new contract. Check your contract to see how long the roll-over period is - it can't be more than 12 months. If you're not sure, contact your supplier to check.

If your contract didn't give you a roll-over period or the period has ended, you'll be on an 'out-of-contract' tariff.

If you're in a roll-over period or on an out-of-contract tariff, it's worth switching - they're usually very expensive. You won't need to pay a fee or give notice to switch.

If you can't switch to a different supplier

Your supplier might still let you move to one of their cheaper tariffs - it's worth calling them to check.

It's worth calling your supplier to ask if they can offer you a better deal. They have to tell you if you can move to a cheaper tariff - but you might have to sign a new contract.

Make sure you understand all the rules about any new tariffs they offer you. You'll usually have to agree to sign up for a fixed period of time - most business energy contracts last between 1 to 3 years.

You should check:

how long the new contract is for

how much you'll pay per unit of energy and if the price can change

If you're struggling to pay your bills it's worth asking if your supplier can take other steps to help - for example, by giving you a smart meter so your bills are more accurate.

Don't feel pressured into agreeing to anything over the phone - if you're not sure, ask them to send you the details.

If you can switch you should compare what they've offered with other suppliers' prices.

If you can't switch and your supplier won't offer you a better deal you should check what to do if you're struggling to pay your energy bills.

Check if you can pay less with a new supplier

It's best to compare as many different suppliers' contracts as possible.

You'll normally need to speak to suppliers to compare prices and contracts. If you don't have much time to do this yourself you could use a price comparison website or an energy broker to find you the best deal.

You'll need to give information about what your business does and how much energy you use.

It's worth trying to negotiate with suppliers and brokers - mention other deals you've been offered and ask if they can beat them.

Contacting suppliers directly

Use our customer service rating table to find business energy suppliers that give the best customer service. Make a list of suppliers to contact for quotes.

It's best to call them to find out what prices and contracts they can offer you. You can find their contact details on their websites.

Tell them you're interested in switching and ask what prices and contracts they can offer you. If you've been offered a cheaper price by another supplier it's worth saying - you might be able to get a better deal.

Ask them to send you the full terms and conditions of any contract they can offer you.

Using energy price comparison websites

You can check other suppliers' tariffs using a price comparison website. Not all websites will show the same tariffs and suppliers, so it’s a good idea to check several.

Ofgem has a list of genuine price comparison websites. The list is for ‘domestic’ customers who use their energy at home - but most of the websites also compare tariffs for business users. Check the list of price comparison websites on Ofgem’s website.

If you use a different price comparison website, you should check if it's genuine. Some websites might be scams and offer deals that are too good to be true. Check if something might be a scam.

[...]
You'll normally have to pay a broker. Before you ask them to find you a deal, check how they'll charge you. You might have to pay a one-off fee when you sign up, or pay as part of the cost of your energy while you're in the contract.

You can agree to use a broker over the phone. This agreement is binding - you should always ask for information in writing before agreeing to a contract.

If your broker is paid by your supplier they must be registered with either the Energy Ombudsman or Utilities Intermediaries Association (UIA). Check your broker is registered before you agree to use them - if they aren't registered you won't be able to complain if something goes wrong.

Check which scheme your broker is a member of by checking on the scheme’s website:

[...]
Once you’ve got quotes from a broker you can go back to your current supplier to see if they can offer you a better deal.

If you're a microbusiness customer

Your business might be a microbusiness if it meets certain criteria. You can check if your business is a microbusiness.

You get extra protection if you’re working with a broker that’s paid by your supplier. Your broker is paid by the supplier if they get a set amount or a commission when they work with them.

The broker has to tell you how much the supplier pays them before you agree to a contract. The costs might be a set amount or a commission on how much energy you use.

Your supplier or broker should send you the terms and conditions within 10 days of agreeing a contract. This should include details of any fee your broker will get for arranging your energy contract.

Comparing contracts

When you're comparing the contracts you've been offered, make sure you check:

how much you'll pay per unit of energy and if the price can change

if there are any extra costs - for example, maintenance charges

how long the contract will last for - and if you'll have to pay a fee to cancel it before it ends

how much notice you'll need to give to end the contract

if there's a 'cooling off' period where you can cancel or switch if you're not happy - most business energy suppliers don't offer one but it's worth checking

If you've used a broker to find you a deal make sure you consider their fees when deciding whether to sign up to a contract. For example, it might be a one-off charge that you pay your broker or it might be added to your energy bill. The broker must give you this information in writing.

If you’re agreeing a contract

Always ask suppliers to send you a written contract so you can check the terms and conditions before you agree to anything.

Business energy contracts are 'binding' if you agree to them over the phone - this means you don't need to sign anything to be tied in to the contract.

Switching

If you've decided to switch you should tell the company that already supplies your energy as soon as possible.

You'll need to agree to your contract with the new supplier and confirm when they'll take over supplying you with energy.

It's important to take accurate meter readings on the day you switch and send them to both companies so you pay the right amount.

You'll be switched to your new supplier within 5 working days. If you want to switch on a specific date, contact your new supplier to ask if you can do this. For example, you might want to do this if you’re on a fixed-term contract and don’t want to switch until it ends.

You won't get a cooling-off period when you switch. Only switch when you’ve looked at all the information and are clear on the terms of the contract. If you change your mind you might have to pay a termination fee.

Check what your broker is getting paid for setting up the contract

Check your contract with your energy supplier or ask your supplier to tell you what your broker is getting for setting up the contract.

You should ask your supplier to explain how the broker is paid - for example, money from every unit of energy your business uses. You can compare this with what your broker told you they were getting.

The amount of detail your supplier must tell you depends on what type of business you are.

If you're a microbusiness
If you’re not a microbusiness

If your broker has misled you, you can complain. For example, your broker might have misled you about the terms of your contract or your tariff being the cheapest.

If you complain, you might be able to cancel your contract or get your money back.

Contacting your supplier or broker about a problem

Ofgem confirms greater protection for businesses
Publication type:
Press release
Publication date:
5 April 2024
Topic: Gas supply
Print this page
Share the page
Share on Facebook
Share on X
Share on LinkedIn

Businesses will get fairer treatment, more support resolving disputes and greater transparency on broker fees under new rules announced by Ofgem today.

The changes will apply to the non-domestic energy sector, which includes businesses, public services like sports centres and village halls, utilities, charities and more. The new rules will make sure energy suppliers improve customer service, open doors to alternative dispute resolution schemes and clearly set out costs for businesses, including fees paid for third party services, like energy brokers.

Under the changes, Ofgem will from 1 July 2024:

Expand the Standards of Conduct to apply to all businesses of any size, rather than just Micro Business consumers. This will give Ofgem powers to take action against suppliers that do not treat non-domestic customers fairly.
Introduce a new supply licence rule for non-domestic suppliers which requires them to signpost Micro Business consumers to Citizens Advice and Citizens Advice Scotland, who can offer support and advice when they have an issue. This will also apply to Small Business consumers from December 2024, subject to the new definition entering legislation.

Further changes, that Ofgem expects to be in place by the end of the year, include:

Expanding the requirement for a contract’s principal terms to clearly display any broker fees from Micro Business consumers to all non-domestic customers. This will apply to contracts signed on and from 1 October 2024 and suppliers must make this information available upon request.

From December 2024, in line with the government’s proposed new Small Business consumer definition entering legislation, Ofgem will also:

Update the Complaints Handling Standards to ensure suppliers put in place suitable complaints processes for Small Business consumers and point them to the Energy Ombudsman when a customer does not feel the issue has been resolved.
Implement a requirement for suppliers to only work with Third-party Intermediaries (TPIs), often referred to as brokers, that are members of a redress scheme when securing Small Business contracts. This will provide reassurance to business customers that they are able to access dispute resolution schemes and get a fair and suitable outcome.

Tim Jarvis, Ofgem’s Director General for Markets, said:

"Too many businesses have experienced issues with some energy suppliers, from difficulty getting the right contracts, unexplained price hikes, and poor customer service.

“We’ve worked hard to understand the breadth of issues and where the powers we have to tackle them can be improved. These new rules will help ensure businesses get the service they deserve.

“We’ll be speaking to businesses of all sizes as these rules come into force throughout this year to make sure they are being followed by suppliers. We’ll also continue to work with government, industry, and consumer groups to see what else can be done to support non-domestic consumers.”

Ofgem’s new rules come as the government confirms plans to expand its definition of Small Businesses, meaning businesses with less than 50 employees and a certain turnover or using a certain amount of energy can take complaints about their energy supplier to the Energy Ombudsman.

Under new Ofgem rules, Small Businesses will also be able to resolve disputes about third parties like energy brokers with redress scheme providers, such as the Energy Ombudsman and the Utilities Intermediaries Association (UIA). This was previously only available for Micro Business consumers so the change will give more businesses access to independent support with complaints.

The changes being brought in by Ofgem to help businesses result from concerns shared last year about problems including poor customer service and complaint handling from those in the non-domestic energy market. This prompted a joint deep dive to learn more about these issues with the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero (DESNZ), the full results of which have now been published.

More than half of those taking part in the research (58%) said they were concerned about the impact of energy prices on their business, with 42% reporting they were very concerned. And almost two thirds (60%) of businesses were satisfied with the overall service they had received from their supplier, with 13% saying that they were dissatisfied.

The main reasons consumers said they were dissatisfied included the service being too expensive, poor customer service, and poor communication from their supplier.

NOTES TO EDITORS
A Micro Business consumer uses less than 100,000 kWh of electricity a year; uses less than 293,000 kWh of gas a year; or has fewer than 10 employees (or their full-time equivalent) and an annual turnover total not exceeding 2 million Euros (equivalent to £1.716m according on 22 March 2024).
Today’s announcement aligns with the new Government definition of Small Business and support from the Energy Ombudsman to cover businesses with fewer than 50 employees and an annual turnover of £6.5 million or a balance sheet total of £5 million; or an annual electricity consumption level of 200,000kWh; or an annual gas consumption level of 500,000 kWh.
We are currently aware of two redress schemes in operation which can provide support in resolving consumers' disputes with an energy broker:
The Energy Ombudsman
The Utilities Intermediaries Association (UIA)
The new changes being introduced follow from a Call for Input on the Non-Domestic Gas and Electricity Market and a Non-Domestic Market Review Findings and Policy Consultation. The statutory consultation on the proposals ended earlier this year.
We recently published a report of findings from research conducted with non-domestic energy customers. This research was commissioned by Ofgem and DESNZ to build on existing evidence about non-domestic consumers’ experiences of the energy market.
